Brute Force.summary: Repeated password guessing against accounts or services.
steps: Rate-limit login attempts and lock accounts after a small number of failures (for example 5 in 10 minutes).
Enforce multi-factor authentication on exposed services, especially VPN, webmail and SSH.
Disable password authentication for SSH in favour of key pairs.
Block or challenge the offending source IPs at the firewall or edge proxy.
Review accounts that logged in successfully shortly after many failures; assume compromise if the pattern repeats.

Port Scan.summary: Systematic probing of ports or services to map what is reachable.
steps: Confirm which of the touched ports actually host services; close the ones that should not be public.
Restrict management ports (SSH, RDP, databases) to known networks with firewall rules.
Rate-limit or tarpit repeated connection attempts from single sources.
Move service banners and version responses behind authentication where possible so scanning learns less.

Malware Activity.summary: Suspicious code execution, encoded payloads or malware-style file activity.
steps: Isolate the affected host from the network before doing anything else.
Search other machines for the same file names, scheduled tasks or registry/service changes.
Force a password reset for every account that logged into the affected host recently.
Rebuild the host from a known-good image rather than attempting in-place cleanup.
Block the external destinations contacted; consider sinking hole the domains outright.

SQL Injection.summary: Database manipulation attempted through web input fields.
steps: Parameterise every database query; never build SQL by string concatenation with request data.
Review web server and database logs to check whether any injection attempt actually returned data.
Rotate database credentials that were reachable from the affected application.
Add a WAF rule or input validation for quotes, semicolons and SQL keywords in query strings.
Give the application account the smallest possible database rights (no schema changes, no file access).

Privilege Escalation.summary: Attempts to gain higher-level permissions than the account holds.
steps: Remove unneeded sudo/group memberships and audit who currently holds administrative rights.
Patch or remove the tools and setuid binaries involved; check the host against vendor advisories.
Review recent logins by the affected accounts and rotate their credentials.
Alert on future writes to sensitive files such as /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow or the Windows SAM.
Restrict interactive logins for service accounts entirely.

DoS Indicators.summary: Traffic or request patterns aimed at exhausting capacity.
steps: Apply rate limits per source IP at the load balancer or reverse proxy.
Reduce per-request cost: cache aggressively, cap request body sizes, tighten timeouts.
Contact the upstream provider about scrubbing or blackhole routing if saturation is real.
Scale the affected service horizontally while investigating the source of the load.
